In the electronics lab, Pema's group had finished early, so she stayed to watch Akash's group put their smart-irrigation project together for the next morning's demo.
Akash had written the code for the soil sensor. Neha had built the pump control. Joel had made the display. Each part worked on its own; Pema had seen them all test it.
At seven they connected everything. The display showed "moisture: 812." The pump expected a percentage. It stayed off. Neha said, "I thought the sensor sent percent." Akash said, "Nobody told me that." Joel's display was also set for a different pin.
Pema watched them sit in silence under the tube light. She felt a knot in her stomach; her own group had nearly done the same thing in the first year.
They stayed till midnight rewriting. Pema, leaving, thought: one meeting on day one, one test at the halfway point, and they'd be asleep now.

Dear Kavya,
You start college next week, and you said you have a group project in the first term. Let me tell you what I watched happen to my roommate's group last semester.
Dilnaz and three others had to build a small website for a local bakery. They split it up on the first day: one did the menu page, one the order form, one the design, Dilnaz the database. Then they worked separately for five weeks.
The night before submission they put it together in our room. The order form sent "name, phone." The database expected "first name, last name, mobile." The design used different colours from the menu page. Dilnaz sat on her bed saying, "But it all worked on my laptop." I made them tea at 2 a.m.
They submitted it half broken.
So, one thing: in the first week, agree how the pieces will talk to each other, and put them together once, halfway.
Mohit

You asked on the podcast about group work. I'm Sharmila, and the best lesson I got was from watching my cousin Urmila's film project at her college.
Four of them. One wrote the script, one shot the video, one did the music, one edited. They met on day one and then just… went off. Urmila was the editor, so everything landed on her laptop the night before.
I was staying with her that week. The video was shot in portrait, on phones. The music was four minutes; the film was six. The script had a scene nobody had filmed. Urmila kept saying, "Why didn't anyone check?" and nobody had, including her.
I remember sitting on the floor next to her at 1 a.m., feeling so helpless. They cut it into something, but it wasn't the film they'd planned.
Now at my job, the first thing I ask is: what does each piece hand to the next? And when do we try joining them?

qa.q: How long was the music, and how long was the film?
qa.a: The music was four minutes; the film was six.

qa.q: How did Sharmila feel sitting next to Urmila at 1 a.m.?
qa.a: Sharmila felt helpless and sympathetic, watching the pieces fail to fit.

qa.q: What two questions does Sharmila now ask at work, and why?
qa.a: What each piece hands to the next and when to try joining them, because Urmila's group never agreed or checked until the last night.

qa.q: How might Urmila feel as the editor that night?
qa.a: Urmila was probably overwhelmed and frustrated, with every mismatched part landing on her laptop at once.

I'm Bidisha, and I share a hostel room with Urmila, so I watched the whole thing from my bed. Her group of three had split the robotics project two weeks earlier: Urmila wrote the sensor code, Rohan built the motor board, Aarti made the chassis. They met again only the night before the demo.
Around eleven the laptop was plugged in and the robot sat on our floor. It jerked forward and crashed into my cupboard. Urmila's code sent distances in centimetres; Rohan's board expected metres. Then Aarti's chassis turned out to be too narrow for Rohan's battery.
Nobody shouted, but nobody said much either. Urmila kept rubbing her eyes. Rohan said, "I thought we'd agreed on metres," and Urmila said, "When?"
They worked till three with tape and a converted number. I can't say what each of them was thinking. I only know one short test run in the first week would have shown all of it.
